text:
A Bullion Trading Tradition
Silver at 25 · Gold at 50
Anniversary Gifts by Year — Silver, Gold & the Metal Milestones
For more than a century, couples have marked each year of marriage with a chosen material — fragile paper at the first, enduring gold at the fiftieth. Here is the complete year-by-year list, the metal milestones, and the custom of engraving a keepsake that holds its value for a lifetime.
Educational only — anniversary lists vary between sources; the metal milestones are the most consistent.
ANNIVERSARY
For more than a century, couples have marked each year of marriage with a chosen material — fragile paper at the first, enduring gold at the fiftieth. It is one of the few gift customs where the symbol itself grows
more precious, and more permanent
, the longer love lasts.
This is the complete guide: the full year-by-year list (traditional and modern), the four metal milestones every family remembers — silver at 25, gold at 50 — the gemstone years, and the old custom of engraving a keepsake that outlasts the party.
The silver milestone
25th
The silver anniversary — traceable to the German “silberne Hochzeit,” the silver wreath
The gold milestone
50th
The golden anniversary — gold wreaths for 50 years, the oldest, most universal milestone
List expanded
1937
The U.S. National Retail Jeweler Association filled the tradition out to nearly every year
Where the tradition comes from
The custom is older than the printed lists. In
medieval and early-modern Germany
, a wife who reached her 25th anniversary was crowned with a
silver wreath
; at 50 years, a
gold wreath
. Those two ceremonies — the
silberne Hochzeit
and
goldene Hochzeit
— are widely cited as the ancestors of today’s anniversary guides, and they explain why 25 is silver and 50 is gold to this day.
The idea was well established in English-speaking custom by the mid-1800s: the 1859
Old Farmer’s Almanac
already counted off paper, wood, tin, silver, gold, and diamond. In
1922
, etiquette author
Emily Post
printed an influential list in her book
Etiquette
, and in
1937 the American National Retail Jeweler Association
extended the tradition to cover nearly every year. (A popular story credits public libraries with fielding so many stumped-spouse letters that a complete list became a public service — charming lore rather than firmly documented history.)

The metal milestones and the color associated with each.
25 · SILVER — 50 · GOLD
Silver at 25, gold at 50 — the two milestones the whole tradition is built around.
Between the metal milestones sits a run of gemstone years, each with a color that makes gift and décor planning easy:
Ruby at 40
(red),
Sapphire at 45
(blue),
Alexandrite (or emerald) at 55
,
Diamond at 60
(the “Diamond Jubilee” year),
Blue Sapphire at 65
, and
Diamond again at 75
. The tradition reads as a slow crescendo — fragile paper and cotton at the start, then the metals and stones — each material a little stronger and more valuable, mirroring a marriage that has been tested and has held.
The custom of engraving a keepsake
Engraving is what turns a symbolic material into a personal heirloom. Couples have engraved rings, watches, and silver with dates and initials for generations, and the appeal is simple: a specific date or set of initials gives an object a permanence that no generic gift can match. The most popular engravings are the
wedding date
(often in Roman numerals), the couple’s
initials or names
, a short line or vow, or the
coordinates
of where they met or married.
That is the real argument for metal over most anniversary gifts. Precious metals
endure
(they don’t fade, rot, or break), they are
tangible and portable
, and — unlike almost every other anniversary gift — they
hold real, liquid value
. An engraved silver round or gold bar is at once a keepsake and a small store of value: the literal version of “your love is as good as gold.”

The engravable Liberty Eagle round has a blank central medallion made to be personalized with a date or initials — a full ounce of silver turned into a one-of-a-kind heirloom.

Anniversary etiquette treats the material as a prompt, not a rule — mixing the traditional and modern lists is completely accepted.
Common Questions
Questions families ask us
What is the 25th wedding anniversary gift?
Silver. The 25th is the “silver anniversary,” the first true precious-metal milestone. The associated color is silver/white. It’s the classic occasion for a silver keepsake — an engravable silver round, a Silver Eagle, or a silver bar.
What is the 50th anniversary gift?
Gold. The 50th is the “golden anniversary,” the oldest and most universal milestone, with an associated color of gold/yellow. A gold coin or gold bar is the natural gift — a tangible, lasting way to say fifty years was worth its weight.
What metal is the 70th anniversary?
Platinum. The 70th is the platinum anniversary — the rarest named milestone. Platinum is rarer than gold and was never used as everyday circulating currency, which makes it a fitting symbol for a marriage beyond ordinary measure. The 75th traditionally returns to diamond, sometimes paired with gold.
What’s the difference between the traditional and modern lists?
The traditional list descends from 19th-century custom and was popularized by Emily Post’s 1922 book Etiquette. The modern list was assembled and updated by the jewelry trade in the 20th century, filling in every year and swapping some themes (for example, diamond jewelry for the 10th in place of tin). Neither is more correct — most couples mix them.
Where did the anniversary tradition come from?
Its roots are usually traced to medieval Germany, where a wife’s 25th anniversary was marked with a silver wreath and the 50th with a gold wreath. The gift list was already circulating in English-speaking custom by 1859 (in The Old Farmer’s Almanac), was popularized by Emily Post in 1922, and was expanded to cover nearly every year by the American National Retail Jeweler Association in 1937.
Why is engraving traditional for anniversary keepsakes?
A specific date or set of initials gives an object a permanence a generic gift can’t match. Couples have engraved rings, watches, and silver with wedding dates and initials for generations. On a precious-metal piece, the engraving fixes the memory to something that will outlast the party and can be handed down as an heirloom.
What should I engrave on an anniversary keepsake?
The most popular choices are the wedding date (often in Roman numerals), the couple’s initials or names, a short line or vow, or the coordinates of where they met or married. Keep it short — a date and two sets of initials read beautifully on a silver round.
Why give precious metal instead of a traditional gift?
Three reasons: it endures (metal doesn’t fade, rot, or break), it’s tangible and portable, and — unlike almost every other anniversary gift — it holds real, liquid value. An engraved silver round or gold bar is both a keepsake and a small store of value: the literal version of “your love is as good as gold.”
What are the gemstone anniversary years?
The headline gem years are Ruby at 40 (red), Sapphire at 45 (blue), Alexandrite at 55 (some modern lists say emerald), Diamond at 60 (white), Blue Sapphire at 65, and Diamond again at 75. Colors track the stones, which makes party and flower themes easy.
How much should I spend on a milestone anniversary?
There’s no rule. Etiquette treats the material as a prompt, not an obligation. In practice, many people treat a 25th or 50th like a landmark birthday and spend more precisely because the occasion is rare and the keepsake is meant to last. A silver keepsake can start under $100; a gold milestone piece scales with the spot price of gold.
Marking a 25th or 50th?
Match the metal to the milestone — a personalized, engravable silver round for a Silver 25th, a gold bar or Gold Eagle for a Golden 50th, and fractional gold for the years in between. Everything is in stock, and we ship nationwide.
